paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The permafrost carbon cycle, also called the Arctic carbon cycle, is a smaller loop inside Earth's global carbon cycle. Permafrost is material below the ground surface that stays under 0ᵒ C (32ᵒ F) for at least two years in a row. The cycle follows carbon as it moves out of permafrost soils into plants and microbes, up into the atmosphere, back into plants, and at last back into permafrost, buried as sediment by freezing-related processes.

paragraphs.heading: A huge frozen store
paragraphs.text: Because these soils stay frozen for so long, they lock away large amounts of carbon and other nutrients. Soils in general are the biggest carbon stores in land ecosystems, and that is also true of Arctic soils sitting on permafrost. Soils affected by permafrost cover nearly 9% of Earth's land, yet they hold between 25 and 50% of all soil organic carbon. Estimates of this store come to more than twice the carbon now in the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Locking carbon in
paragraphs.text: Permafrost does not make carbon. Carbon from plants has to be worked into the soil and then into the permafrost before it is really stored. One route is syngenetic permafrost growth: the ground surface rises as wind-blown or river-borne sediment and peat pile up, and the new soil becomes part of the permafrost as its top rises. Since permafrost responds slowly to climate change, carbon stored this way stays out of the air for long periods, and radiocarbon dating shows it is often thousands of years old.

paragraphs.heading: Mixing by frost
paragraphs.text: The second route is cryoturbation, the churning of soil by repeated freezing and thawing. It carries carbon from the surface down to deeper levels of the soil, and frost heaving is its most common form. In time, carbon that started at the surface sinks far enough into the active layer to join the permafrost. When this churning works together with the build-up of sediment, carbon is stored faster.

paragraphs.heading: How much is there
paragraphs.text: Soil organic carbon in the northern circumpolar permafrost region comes to an estimated 1,460–1,600 Pg; one Pg equals one Gt, or 10¹⁵g. Counting the Tibetan Plateau too, the permafrost of the Northern Hemisphere likely holds around 1832 Gt. Estimates put about 200 Pg in the top 30 cm, about 500 Pg in the top 100 cm, and about 1024 Pg in the top 300 cm. More lies below 3 m, in yedoma, thick carbon-rich silt found across Siberia and in parts of North America (400 Pg), and in delta deposits across the Arctic (240 Pg).

paragraphs.heading: Thaw and warming
paragraphs.text: This vast store raises many concerns, and until recently climate models and global carbon budgets left it out. As climate change warms the Arctic, thaw spreads and the active layer deepens, exposing carbon stored for decades to millennia to living processes that help it enter the atmosphere. The volume of permafrost in the top 3 m of ground is expected to shrink by about 25% for each 1 °C (1.8 °F) of global warming. The IPCC reports high confidence that recent warming has raised permafrost temperatures widely, with parts of Northern Alaska warming as much as 3 °C (5.4 °F) between the early 1980s and the mid-2000s.
